video_title: Bill Ackman: Is Permanent Capital an Investor’s Biggest Edge? | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: Bill Ackman tells Nicolai Tangen that permanent capital is the key edge for concentrated long-term investing in a market made ever shorter-term by multi-manager leverage, indexation and AI, where quality compounders now fall 30-40% on misses. He details turning Howard Hughes into a Buffett-style specialty insurer (80%+ insurance in a decade, float in T-bills, surplus in stocks) and notes Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, bought on tariff/capex selloffs, are about a third of Pershing's portfolio.

insights.claim: Ackman argues most asset-management capital is short-term redeemable (daily/quarterly/annual), which makes long-horizon concentrated investing structurally hard; permanent capital is scarce and is a huge competitive advantage ('time arbitrage').
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Capital structure, not stock-picking skill alone, determines who can harvest long-term mispricings.
insights.quote: the ability to be a long-term investor in a short-term world really exists for us because of our capital base

insights.claim: Ackman says multi-manager platforms like Citadel and Millennium are very short-term oriented and use high financial leverage, so they cannot absorb the volatility a concentrated long-term strategy requires.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Pod-shop dominance creates repeatable dislocations that patient capital can exploit.
insights.quote: You can't absorb a high degree of volatility in a strategy like that.

insights.claim: Because Pershing Square did not face month-end redemptions, it could deploy capital very aggressively during the COVID market meltdown.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Permanent capital converts crises into buying opportunities rather than forced selling.
insights.quote: we could be very aggressively deploying capital uh because we weren't worried about redemptions at the end of the month

insights.claim: Ackman claims one of the biggest sources of market opportunity is that the vast majority of asset managers have capital that can be pulled, combined with herd-like human fear that drives selling at the bottom.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Redemption-driven selling is a durable source of mispricing.
insights.quote: among the things that create the best opportunities in markets is the fact that the vast majority of asset managers have have capital that can can get pulled

insights.claim: Ackman recounts that Warren Buffett in 1969 gave up a 25%-over-6% promote on a ~$100 million hedge fund, returned capital, and took control of Berkshire's textile mills at a $100,000 salary to gain permanent capital.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Trading fee economics for permanent capital is the Buffett template Ackman is copying.

themes.theme: Howard Hughes as a Berkshire-style insurer

insights.claim: Ackman plans to pull as much capital as possible out of Howard Hughes' real estate operation, make it asset-light, and reinvest in an insurance operation, predicting it will be 80%+ insurance and ~20% real estate within a decade.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Howard Hughes is being repositioned from a real estate developer into a Berkshire-like compounding vehicle.
insights.quote: in a decade from now, it will be 80 plus% insurance company and maybe 20% real estate

insights.claim: Ackman says the market assigns Howard Hughes a high cost of capital that is hard to exceed in a real estate operation, which motivates the shift toward insurance.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Explains the strategic rationale for redeploying cash away from master-planned communities.

insights.claim: Upon closing the insurer acquisition in June, Pershing Square sold its intermediate and longer-term fixed income, moved float into short-term Treasuries, and invested a portion of the insurer's equity in a common-stock portfolio.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Mirrors Buffett's float/surplus split: float in T-bills, surplus in equities.

insights.claim: Ackman explains Buffett's model: float from writing policies went into short-term Treasuries while the insurer's surplus went into common stocks, enabling a 20%+ ROE insurer that built most of Berkshire's value.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: The template for Howard Hughes' insurance strategy.

insights.claim: Ackman says Howard Hughes recruited an insurance team (Mark Brenesen, formerly of Arch Capital Group, his protege David Gansburg, and former AIG vice chair and general counsel Lucy Fetto) normally suited to a $50-100 billion insurer to run a less-than-$2 billion-capital specialty insurer.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Overbuilt talent suggests ambitions to scale the insurer well beyond its current size.
insights.quote: We have a team that you would normally put into a 50 hundred billion dollar insurance operation running a you know not quite $2 billion capital uh insurance company.

insights.claim: Ackman contrasts his model with Apollo, which uses a fixed-annuity life insurer as a low-cost financing vehicle for levered private credit spread investing; Howard Hughes instead bought a specialty P&C insurer/reinsurer that takes underwriting risk with much lower leverage.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Distinguishes Ackman's vehicle from the alt-manager insurance-spread playbook and its credit risk.
insights.quote: it's not a levered spread business

insights.claim: Ackman defines a great company as one you could buy today, have markets shut for 20 years, and still be highly confident you own something enormously valuable.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: A practical filter for long-duration quality.
insights.quote: The markets could shut for 20 years and you know with a enormous degree of certainty that you'll own something that's enormously valuable 10 or 20 years from now.

insights.claim: Ackman prefers royalty-like, annuity-style businesses whose cash flows grow at high rates for long periods and do not need to be reinvested in the business.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Business structure matters more than sector.

insights.claim: Ackman estimates there are only about a couple hundred to 300 truly great businesses globally, and they rarely trade at prices that make them great investments, which is why Pershing Square runs a concentrated portfolio of 12-14 positions.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Scarcity of quality at a good price justifies concentration.

insights.claim: Pershing Square's checklist requires high predictability of cash flows over 10-20 years, a durable moat, and avoidance of commodity-, interest-rate- and regulatory-sensitive businesses.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Explicit exclusion list narrows the investable universe sharply.
insights.quote: we don't really invest in commodity sensitive businesses interest rate sensitive businesses regulatory sensitive businesses

insights.claim: Ackman says restaurants have been good investments because franchise models are simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative royalty collectors, citing McDonald's as also a real estate and franchising business.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Look past the sector label to the underlying economic structure.

insights.claim: Ackman rates CEO quality as less important than business quality, growth and durability, noting great businesses usually reach attractive prices because management made mistakes and Pershing can help recruit a better CEO.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Bad management at a great business is an opportunity, not a disqualifier.
insights.quote: Usually it's a great business that gets to an attractive price because management has made a series of mistakes.

insights.claim: Ackman says the best way to gain conviction is to find the best short seller on a position you own and rebut each of their arguments.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Systematic steelmanning of the bear case as a risk-control tool.
insights.quote: Find the best short seller in something that you own and and hear your their arguments. If you can rebut each of their arguments, then you can feel more confident in your investment.

themes.theme: Market structure: volatility, indexation, AI short-termism

insights.claim: Ackman observes that a high-quality company that disappoints can now fall 30-40% on an earnings miss versus 3-4% historically, which he attributes to rising indexation shrinking float and more leveraged short-term capital.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Earnings-miss drawdowns in quality compounders are the key entry point for long-term buyers.
insights.quote: Today the stock could drop 30 or 40% on a miss.

insights.claim: Ackman believes AI is making market participants ever shorter-term, since AI can read a 10-K instantly and huge capital chases short-term edge.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Short-term informational edge is being commoditised; long-horizon analysis becomes relatively more valuable.
insights.quote: I think it's making market participants increasingly shorter and shorter term.

insights.claim: Ackman does not think beating the market is harder now than when he started, because concentration plus a long-term view remains a big competitive advantage, though the index is an amazing competitor.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Alpha persists for structurally patient capital.

insights.claim: Ackman argues increasing indexation and passive ownership risk weakening management accountability, and cites the dispersal of controlled ownership as contributing to underperformance in the 1970s-early 80s before activism rose.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Activism serves as a governance check in a passive-dominated market.

themes.theme: Big Tech AI positions bought on disappointment

insights.claim: Pershing Square bought Amazon after Trump's 'Liberation Day' tariffs, Meta after it disappointed investors with large capex commitments, and Microsoft similarly; these names are about a third of the portfolio.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Roughly one-third portfolio exposure to hyperscalers bought on short-term selloffs.
insights.quote: those names represent about a third of our portfolio today

insights.claim: Ackman finds it odd that a company can announce demand so strong it must raise capex well above expectations and its stock still falls, which he used as an entry point into Microsoft.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Capex-driven selloffs in demand-constrained hyperscalers are buying opportunities in his view.

insights.claim: Ackman says every business today is either AI-related, should be, or will be disrupted by AI, making that the central assessment for any investment.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: AI disruption risk is now a gating diligence question across all sectors.
insights.quote: every business today is either AI related or should be or is going to be disrupted by by AI

insights.claim: Pershing Square holds Brookfield after a several-month diligence process, attracted as it became a more asset-light royalty-collecting business whose complexity keeps it attractively valued.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Complexity discount plus simplification is the thesis.
insights.quote: Brookfield's actually quite a complicated company. That's one of the

insights.claim: Ackman expects AI to give almost everyone access to very low-cost high intelligence, commoditising intelligence and leaving creativity as the main human edge, while driving an explosion of entrepreneurship and GDP growth.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: If intelligence commoditises, value shifts to creativity and to businesses with non-intelligence moats.
insights.quote: I think there's going to be explosion of entrepreneurship

insights.claim: Ackman predicts that AI-enabled brain signal interpretation via brain-computer interfaces will let the blind see and paraplegics walk within years rather than many years.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Signals an emerging area he is studying and that 'may lead to some interesting investment opportunities.'
insights.quote: it's a matter of not months but years but not too many years

insights.claim: Ackman has assembled a 3.4-acre New York site with a 400,000 sq ft biotech building for a brain rehabilitation and recovery institute, arguing neurologists are often nihilistic and the field is underfunded.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Large philanthropic capital entering neuro-rehab/BCI research.

insights.claim: Ackman says the US cannot slow down AI development because an adversary reaching superintelligence first would be dangerous, and the US should maintain preeminent military, AI and nuclear capability.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Supports a continued state-backed AI arms race framing.
insights.quote: I don't know that we can slow down on AI because imagine if [snorts] you know one of our enemies gets to super intelligence.

insights.claim: Ackman says Pershing Square's last activist campaign was launched in 2016; today CEOs typically send thank-you notes when it takes a stake, so it acts as a constructive owner rather than running proxy fights.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Activism has shifted to collaborative engagement backed by reputation.

insights.claim: Ackman prefers one-share-one-vote and generally avoids controlled companies, but accepts founder control under a phenomenal CEO such as Buffett, Sam Walton or Elon Musk, worrying about succession to heirs.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Dual-class structures are acceptable only while the founder is exceptional.
insights.quote: I like one share one vote

insights.claim: Ackman recounts that Carl Icahn owed Pershing about $4.5 million under 'schmuck insurance' from a 1998 Hallwood Realty deal, delayed payment for 6-7 years through appeals, and later squeezed Pershing's Herbalife short, which lost about a billion dollars.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Shows short-squeeze risk when a well-capitalised adversary takes the other side.

insights.claim: Ackman calls X his most important information source, following ~1,000 people with diverging views, and says X users are typically one to two weeks ahead of conventional media.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Real-time social information flow is a practical edge in his process.
insights.quote: you generally feel like you're a week to two weeks ahead like news comes out and you you learned it a week ago

insights.claim: Ackman blames Facebook and engagement-driven social media for polarisation and proposes X add a button surfacing the best opposing argument on any tweet.
insights.speaker: Bill Ackman
insights.so_what: Signals advocacy for product changes at X.
